source: CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: Grain must be dried to below 14% moisture as quickly as possible after harvest to stop ongoing respiration in the grain pile, which otherwise raises the pile's internal temperature and moisture, creating ideal conditions for storage insects and quality loss (broken/discolored grain, off-flavor cooked rice, and reduced seed germination for grain kept as seed). Two drying methods are used. Sun-drying is the traditional, low-cost method requiring only labor, spreading grain over a mat, tarpaulin, or (for larger volumes) a paved/concrete surface. Layer thickness is critical: the ideal thickness is 2–3 cm; thicker layers dry more slowly, crack more grain, and take longer overall. Turning frequency should match sunlight conditions at a constant 2–3 cm thickness: on a clear, fully sunny day, dry for about 1 day, turning every half hour; on a partly sunny day, dry for about 2 days, turning about once an hour; on a mostly overcast/weak-sun day, dry for about 3 days, turning about every 2 hours. Concrete-surface drying is roughly twice as fast as mat/tarpaulin drying in equivalent sun conditions but yields the same final grain/seed quality — except that grain thickness is what actually controls drying time and grain quality, not the drying surface material itself. Mechanical drying uses a rice dryer burning husk and firewood as fuel. A small-scale dryer developed by CARDI, suited to a group of 5–10 households sharing one unit, can dry about 2 tonnes of paddy per 10-hour batch (about 4 tonnes per 24-hour day-and-night of continuous operation), with the grain pile stirred/turned every 4–5 hours during drying; there are two general designs, one where grain flows continuously through a stream of heated air and one where heated air is blown through a stationary bin of grain, with larger commercial-scale versions of both existing alongside the small household-cooperative scale unit. Mechanically dried grain gives noticeably better milling quality than sun-dried grain — about 3 kg more white/head rice recovered per 100 kg of paddy — because mechanical drying is not weather-dependent and gives more even, controlled drying. Mechanical drying is especially useful for farmers growing flood-recession rice, lower-terrace rice, an early-wet-season crop, or an early dry-season crop, all of which routinely mature during periods when reliable sunny-day drying weather cannot be counted on.
